final_proof:
The claim as written is false. The failure is caused by the displayed series starting at n = 1, even though the enumerations start with j₀ and k₀: the two series can omit different nonzero terms.

Take I = J = K = ℕ₀, V = ℝ, and set v₀ = 1, v₁ = 2, and vᵢ = 0 for i ≥ 2. Then {i ∈ I : vᵢ ≠ 0} = {0,1} ⊆ J ∩ K. Let jₙ = n for all n ≥ 0, and let k₀ = 1, k₁ = 0, and kₙ = n for n ≥ 2. Both are bijective enumerations of ℕ₀, but

  ∑_{n=1}^∞ v_{jₙ} = 2,    whereas    ∑_{n=1}^∞ v_{kₙ} = 1.

Both series are absolutely convergent. Moreover, their sums of norms are also respectively 2 and 1. Hence, whether “converges absolutely to r” means that the vector series has sum r and is absolutely convergent, or that the series of norms has sum r, taking r = 2 makes the left side true and the right side false.

Here is a corrected, stronger statement. Under the hypotheses in the problem, replace both lower bounds n = 1 by n = 0. Then

  ∑_{n=0}^∞ ‖v_{jₙ}‖ = ∑_{n=0}^∞ ‖v_{kₙ}‖                                           (1)

as extended nonnegative real numbers. If this common value is finite, both vector series converge and have the same sum in V. Consequently, for every r ∈ ℝ_{>0}, either usual interpretation of the intended corrected claim is valid (with the vector-sum interpretation requiring r to be identified with an element of V).

Proof of the correction. Put S = {i ∈ I : vᵢ ≠ 0}. Suppose first that

  A := ∑_{n=0}^∞ ‖v_{jₙ}‖ < ∞.

For every M ≥ 0, terms outside S vanish, and hence

  ∑_{m=0}^M ‖v_{kₘ}‖ = ∑_{0≤m≤M, kₘ∈S} ‖v_{kₘ}‖.

Every kₘ ∈ S lies in J, so it equals a unique jₙ. Since both enumerations are injective, the terms on the right correspond to distinct terms of the nonnegative series defining A. Therefore

  ∑_{m=0}^M ‖v_{kₘ}‖ ≤ A.

The partial sums on the left are nondecreasing and bounded, so their limit B := ∑_{m=0}^∞ ‖v_{kₘ}‖ exists and satisfies B ≤ A. Now the same argument with J,(jₙ) and K,(kₙ) interchanged applies because B < ∞, and gives A ≤ B. Thus A = B. By symmetry, if the k-series of norms is initially assumed finite, the same conclusion follows. In particular, one norm sum is finite if and only if the other is, and then they are equal; if neither is finite, both sides of (1) are +∞. This proves (1) and proves that absolute convergence in either enumeration is equivalent to absolute convergence in the other with the same absolute sum.

For completeness, we prove that the vector sums also agree. Suppose the common value in (1) is finite and write A_N = ∑_{n=0}^N v_{jₙ}. For q > p,

  ‖A_q − A_p‖ ≤ ∑_{n=p+1}^q ‖v_{jₙ}‖.

The right side tends to zero as p tends to infinity, so (A_N) is Cauchy. Because V is Banach, A_N converges to some x ∈ V. Put B_M = ∑_{m=0}^M v_{kₘ}.

Let ε > 0. Choose N such that

  ‖A_N − x‖ < ε/2    and    ∑_{n>N} ‖v_{jₙ}‖ < ε/2.

The finite set F = {jₙ : 0 ≤ n ≤ N and v_{jₙ} ≠ 0} lies in S ⊆ K. Since (kₘ) enumerates K, there is M₀ such that every member of F occurs among k₀,…,k_{M₀}. For every M ≥ M₀, all the nonzero terms of A_N occur in B_M; any additional nonzero terms of B_M are distinct terms v_{jₙ} with n > N. Thus the triangle inequality yields

  ‖B_M − A_N‖ ≤ ∑_{n>N} ‖v_{jₙ}‖ < ε/2.

Consequently, for every M ≥ M₀,

  ‖B_M − x‖ ≤ ‖B_M − A_N‖ + ‖A_N − x‖ < ε.

Hence B_M → x, so both vector series have the same sum. This proves the corrected statement.
